\chapter{The Two Signs the Rest of the Run Cost}
\label{ch:ja-numbers-six-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say and write one to ten in Japanese, build any number up to ninety-nine out of those ten words, and say which of them carry a second reading and why.}

Run ichi to juu in order, build thirteen and thirty out of the same two words, and say what the ten numbers cost in signs.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nana]{\ja{なな} — seven, and the pattern from four holding}

\label{lesson:JA-C15-nana}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then a number out of order, on purpose.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{four} both ways, and say which is the native one — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my mother} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} take the farewell in all four skills — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

This chapter does not start at six. Six is one of only two numbers left that costs a new sign, and both of those wait until the end.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{なな}} — \emph{nana} — \textbf{seven}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{しち}} — \emph{shichi} — \textbf{seven}, the same number said the other way
\end{quote}

All three signs are yours: \textbf{\ja{な}}, \textbf{\ja{し}}, \textbf{\ja{ち}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the same seam, a second time}]
Wiktionary's readings box for the kanji \textbf{seven} says exactly what the box for \textbf{four} said:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{borrowed reading} & \textbf{native word} \\
\midrule
four & \textbf{\ja{し}} \emph{shi} & \textbf{\ja{よん}} \emph{yon} \\
seven & \textbf{\ja{しち}} \emph{shichi} & \textbf{\ja{なな}} \emph{nana} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Twice now, and both times at a number where the borrowed reading is easy to mishear — \emph{shi} against \emph{ichi}, \emph{shichi} against \emph{ichi}. The native word is the one that keeps the count clear, and it is the one you will hear.

One instance was a fact about four. Two is a pattern, and this is where the book says so.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{なな}}. Say what you have: \emph{ichi, ni, san, yon, go … nana}. Leave the hole where six is; you will hear it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs did this lesson need? (\textbf{None.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B8\%83}{Wiktionary: the kanji read shichi and nana}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%AA\%E3\%81\%AA}{Wiktionary: \ja{なな}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hachi]{\ja{はち} — eight, with nothing standing beside it}

\label{lesson:JA-C15-hachi}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the plain case.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{seven}, both ways — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my elder brother} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{excuse me} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{はち}} — \emph{hachi} — \textbf{eight}
\end{quote}

Two beats, two old signs: \textbf{\ja{は}} from chapter one and \textbf{\ja{ち}} from chapter two.

And that is the whole lesson, which is the point of it. \textbf{Eight has no second name.} Four had one and seven had one; eight does not, and neither did one, two, three or five. The pattern you were shown twice is not everywhere — it sits at two numbers out of the seven you now hold.

A rule you cannot see the edge of is not a rule you can use. This is the edge.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{はち}}. Say what you hold: \emph{ichi, ni, san, yon, go … nana, hachi}. The hole at six is still there.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs did this lesson need? (\textbf{None.})

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%AF\%E3\%81\%A1}{Wiktionary: \ja{はち}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ku]{\ja{く} — nine, and the exception to the seam}

\label{lesson:JA-C15-ku}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then a number with two readings and no native one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eight} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my elder sister} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{み}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{く}} — \emph{ku} — \textbf{nine}
\end{quote}

One mora, one sign, and you have had that sign since chapter nine, where it closed \textbf{\ja{よく}}. Say \emph{hachi, ku}.

Nine has a second everyday reading as well, \emph{kyū}, and it is the commoner of the two. This book cannot spell it yet — it needs two signs you have not met — so it is written here in romanization only and will be spelled when those signs arrive.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — a second reading that is not a native word}]
Four and seven each had two names, and in both the second was the \textbf{native} word. Nine has two names too, and Wiktionary's readings box puts \textbf{both} of them on the borrowed side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{readings the box calls borrowed} & \textbf{the native word} \\
\midrule
four & \textbf{\ja{し}} & \textbf{\ja{よん}} — used \\
seven & \textbf{\ja{しち}} & \textbf{\ja{なな}} — used \\
nine & \textbf{\ja{く}}, \emph{kyū} & \emph{kokono} — not used in the plain count \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the pattern is narrower than it looked two lessons ago: \emph{some} numbers have two everyday names, and only \emph{some of those} get their second name from the native side. Nine has two names for a different reason.

You met the plain case at eight. This is the other edge.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{く}}. Say what you hold: \emph{ichi, ni, san, yon, go … nana, hachi, ku}. Two numbers are missing and you can hear both gaps.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two numbers are still missing? (\textbf{Six and ten} — the two that cost a sign.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B9\%9D}{Wiktionary: the kanji read kyuu and ku}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ro]{\ja{ろ} — one turn, and the r you already make}

\label{lesson:JA-W15-ro}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then one sign.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nine} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my younger brother} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{め}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ろ}} — \emph{ro}
\end{quote}

Write \textbf{\ja{ら}} once. \textbf{\ja{ろ}} starts the same way and ends differently: a short stroke across the top, then down and round to the left and back up, closing the loop instead of leaving a hook.

The sound is the one \textbf{\ja{ら}} already taught you — a single tap of the tongue, neither the English \emph{r} nor the English \emph{l}.

This is the first new sign in two chapters, and it is here for one word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Trace \textbf{\ja{ろ}} once and copy it once.
  \item Hide it; write it after ten seconds.
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{ら}} and \textbf{\ja{ろ}} side by side and say both, one tap each.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Stop after one accurate form.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[roku]{\ja{ろく} — six, and the hole closes}

\label{lesson:JA-C15-roku}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the word the last lesson bought a sign for.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ろ}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my younger sister} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{well, fully} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ろく}} — \emph{roku} — \textbf{six}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ja{ろ}} arrived last lesson; \textbf{\ja{く}} you have had since chapter nine, where it also became the number \textbf{nine}. So the sign \textbf{\ja{く}} does two jobs in this run: it is \emph{nine} on its own and the second beat of \emph{six}.

Six has one everyday reading. No native word stands beside it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — why six waited}]
You have been counting round a gap for three lessons. Here is what the gap was: of the ten numbers in this run, \textbf{exactly two need a sign this book had not taught}, and six is the first of them.

That is why the chapter did not start here. Everything that cost nothing came first, so that when a lesson finally spends a sign you can see exactly what it bought.

Say the run: \emph{ichi, ni, san, yon, go, roku, nana, hachi, ku}. Nine of ten, and only one gap left.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Read \textbf{\ja{ろ} | \ja{く}}. Write \textbf{\ja{ろく}}, hide it, write it again from the meaning. Then say \emph{roku, nana, hachi, ku} four times, without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of the ten numbers cost a new sign? (\textbf{Two} — this one, and one more.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%82\%8D\%E3\%81\%8F}{Wiktionary: \ja{ろく}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[small yu]{\ja{ゅ} — a small sign that joins forward}

\label{lesson:JA-W15-small-yu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the last new sign of the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ゆ}}, full size — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my husband} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{く}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ゅ}} — small \emph{yu}
\end{quote}

Same shape as \textbf{\ja{ゆ}}, written small and sitting low — the way \textbf{\ja{っ}} is a small \textbf{\ja{つ}}.

The two small signs do opposite jobs, and it is worth putting them side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ja{っ}} & holds a silent beat \emph{before} the next consonant \\
\textbf{\ja{ゅ}} & joins to the sign \emph{before} it, and the two become \textbf{one beat} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \textbf{\ja{し}} plus \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} is not \emph{shi-yu}. It is one beat, \emph{shu}. Voice the \textbf{\ja{し}} with the dakuten first and \textbf{\ja{じ}} plus \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} is one beat, \emph{ju}.

That is the sign the last number needs.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{ゆ}}, then \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} beneath it, half the height.
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{っ}} and \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} side by side; say which one holds and which one joins.
  \item Read \textbf{\ja{じゅ}} as a single beat. Do not let a \emph{yu} escape between the two.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Stop after one accurate small form.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jū]{\ja{じゅう} — ten, and what ten does}

\label{lesson:JA-C15-juu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the last number.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ゅ}}, and say what it does to the sign before it — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my wife} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{I do not understand} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{じゅう}} — \emph{jū} — \textbf{ten}
\end{quote}

Three signs, two beats. \textbf{\ja{し}} voiced with the dakuten is \textbf{\ja{じ}}; \textbf{\ja{じ}} with the small \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} is one beat, \emph{ju}; the \textbf{\ja{う}} after it holds that beat long. Say it as two beats, not three: \emph{ju–u}, not \emph{ji-yu-u}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — ten words, ninety-nine numbers}]
\textbf{\ja{じゅう}} is not just the tenth word in a list. It is the one that makes the list go further than itself, and it does so with no joining word at all:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you say} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ja{じゅういち}} & ten, one $\to$ \textbf{eleven} \\
\textbf{\ja{にじゅう}} & two, ten $\to$ \textbf{twenty} \\
\textbf{\ja{にじゅういち}} & two, ten, one $\to$ \textbf{twenty-one} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A number \textbf{before} \ja{じゅう} multiplies it. A number \textbf{after} \ja{じゅう} is added to it. Nothing is inserted between them.

Ten words, and every number up to ninety-nine is one of their arrangements. That is what the last two chapters were for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{じゅう}}. Say the whole run, one to ten, without stopping. Then say \emph{jūichi}, \emph{nijū}, \emph{sanjū}, and build one number of your own between twenty and ninety-nine.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many beats is \textbf{\ja{じゅう}}? (\textbf{Two}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%98\%E3\%82\%85\%E3\%81\%86}{Wiktionary: \ja{じゅう}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{One to ten, and what the run cost}

\label{lesson:JA-R15-six-to-ten}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls before the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten}, in two beats — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{seven}, both ways — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{child} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ど}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here. This is the first time all ten stand in order.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the run}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ichi ni san yon go roku nana hachi ku jū} — without stopping
  \item \emph{Say it:} it again with \textbf{\ja{し}} at four and \textbf{\ja{しち}} at seven
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ja{五}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built in two chapters, in three numbers}]
\textbf{Ten numbers. Two new signs. Ninety-nine numbers you can now say.}

\emph{Ichi} and \emph{go} were yours before chapter fourteen opened. Only \textbf{\ja{ろ}} and \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} had to be bought, one word each.

At \textbf{four} and \textbf{seven} the native word stands beside the borrowed reading; at \textbf{nine} both readings are borrowed, and \textbf{eight} has no second name at all.

\textbf{\ja{五}} is still the only one of the ten you can write as Japanese writes it. The other nine kanji are the next thing this book owes you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs did ten numbers cost? (\textbf{Two}.) Which two numbers have a native word standing beside a borrowed reading? (\textbf{Four and seven}.) What does a number \emph{before} \textbf{\ja{じゅう}} do to it? (\textbf{Multiplies it}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
